newsitem.title: BELGIUM: BELGIAN "ZAIRE" DEBT: FROM TOXIC WASTE TO SAFE BET.
newsitem.headline: BELGIAN "ZAIRE" DEBT: FROM TOXIC WASTE TO SAFE BET.

text.p: Gone are the days when bonds dating from Belgium's colonial past in Zaire (the former Congo) were regarded by investors as toxic waste, the name given to third world debt unlikely ever to be repaid.

This turnaround owes little to the military rebellion presently underway in Zaire, but to an elaborate guarantee scheme which offered investors a chance to get back most of their money after the country gained independence in 1960.
The outstanding paper, offering a tax-free 3.5 percent coupon, now trades on the Brussels stock exchange at a slight premium to its nominal face value. That was not always the case.

When the Democratic Republic of the Congo was established in June 1960, the question of what would be done with the estimated 46 billion francs of colonial debt (denominated in Belgian francs, Congolese francs and dollars) was left unresolved.
Neither side wanted to take responsibility.

Many bonds, when reprinted at the end of World War Two, were stamped Kingdom of Belgium, making them appear like sovereign paper. In fact, under the 1908 colonial act, the Congo had been economically independent from Belgium (issuing separately, helped sometimes by a higher credit rating) and the government in Brussels did not feel bound to honour the debt.
BOND CERTIFICATES SET ON FIRE
Diplomatic relations between Belgium and the new republic soured almost immediately, leaving more than 200,000 private bond holders, mainly Belgians, believing their money was lost.
Some who believed Belgium should take responsibility for the reprinted bonds even burned certificates in disgust in front of the foreign ministry. They probably wished they had not.

By February 1965, relations had thawed enough between the two countries to reach agreement on the division of the debt. One part was assumed by the Congo, another by Belgium and the third, consisting of the Belgian franc and dollar debt not guaranteed by Belgium, by a newly created Belgian-Congolese Redemption and Management Fund.

The Fund issued 11 billion Belgian francs worth of new, 40-year bonds carrying a 3.5 percent tax-free coupon. This paper was offered freely in exchange to holders of the old colonial debt. By June 1966, 94 percent had swapped their holdings.
MOBUTU-FACTOR HITS NEW ISSUE

A month later, the Congo's new leader, the 36-year-old Mobuto Sese Seko, who had seized power in November 1965, renounced the Fund's legality, causing panic among investors. On the Brussels Stock Exchange, the price of the new bonds plunged to just 29 percent of their face value.

It was the start of a troubled period for the Fund. The Congo gradually stopped meeting its share of the Fund's interest payments. In 1971, Belgium assumed the totality of the cost and the Fund broke all links with the recently renamed Zaire.

The price of the bonds remained depressed, rarely trading at more than 60 percent of their face value until the late 1980s, partly because of a second panic among investors in 1977, when Belgium gave new bonds to holders of two Congolese franc issues not covered by the original agreement and to compensate Belgians who had lost property in the former colony.
DIFFERENT STORY IN 1990s
The present Director General of the Fund, Philippe Reul, is however relaxed in his office near Belgium's Parliament.
Thanks to Europe's low interest-rate environment, bearer bonds offering 3.5 percent tax free have become an attractive alternative to Treasury bills and the paper is again in demand.

The Fund took advantage of past moments of price weakness to buy back most of the issue earlier than planned. At June 30, 1996, the end of the Fund's last financial year, only 1.9 billion francs remained in circulation and the fund had surplus cash of 1.2 billion francs invested in short-term money market deposits.

The bonds' steady price performance on the bourse and a decision by the Belgian state -- given the Fund's large reserves -- to stop from January 1, 1996, its annual interest-payment transfers, means intervention is now down to a minimum.
In 1995-96, the official target for early redemptions was 515 million francs, of which only 83 million was in fact bought.
For 1996/97 the target was 216 million. "I have only bought about 56 million francs," Reul said.

Reul said, however, all the Fund's work has not come to a halt. A handful of investors in, or lucky finders of some of the 16 original Congo issues (including a 2.5 percent bond issued in 1887) turn up each year to exercise their right (which was never time limited) to subscribe to the new bonds.
In 1995/96 some 70,000 francs worth of new bonds were issued in this way, taking the total outstanding issue to 10.89 billion francs, or 99.84 percent of its potential maximum.
The Belgian government has also recently assigned the Fund a new task: compensating Belgian nationals who had their businesses "Zairianised" in 1973.

Reul noted that, under the founding statutes, it is technically possible for either Belgium or Zaire to ask the Fund to take on new mandates before its term ends in 2005. So far, however, there have been no contacts with the rebel force led by Laurent-Desire Kabila that has captured 80 percent of the country, he said.
